observations.text: Several tools are available to detect differential gene expression. The predominant approach of different statistical methods is to consider changes in gene expression independent from their genomic context. Previously, DELocal was introduced that takes into consideration gene expression dynamics in the genomic neighbourhood. Whereas DELocal was shown to identify developmentally regulated genes in developing mouse tooth, its performance in other biological conditions remains undetermined. To benchmark DElocal together with other methods, we develop another tool 'broadSeq'. It provides easy to use interface for methods like DELocal , deseq2, limma, edger, EBSeq and many more. Here we report benchmarking results on different data sets that comprise wild type developing mouse organs from different embryonic time points, and also human cancer data. The examined datasets are from the heart, kidney, liver, brain, forebrain, and hindbrain. We found that most methods produce relatively comparable lists of differentially expressed genes. Nevertheless, DELocal identifies partially distinct sets of genes compared to the other methods. Evaluating the identified genes using gene and disease ontology terms show that the uniquely detected genes by DELocal are biologically relevant and also highly expressed compared to the genes identified by the other methods. Because consistently highly expressed genes show relatively subtle fold changes, the neighbourhood concept of DELocal appears to correct for the difficulty in detecting these differential expression of highly expressed genes. Finally, we provide the tools as combined bioconductor packages, allowing researchers to explore and decide the best methods for their data and questions.

metadata.summary: Microexons are extremely short exons that are highly conserved in vertebrates and are essential for normal brain development. Their small size poses a challenge for canonical exon-definition splice site recognition, which typically relies on spliceosomal interactions across standard length exons. Here, we determine the sequence and RNA structural features of neural microexons in humans in comparison with chickens. We find that neural microexons share intronic features that extend the functional distance between the branchpoint and the 3’ splice site, including distal positioning and lengthening of polypyrimidine tracts. Using experimental RNA structure-probing on a subset of neural microexons, we show that the branchpoint-to-splice site region is unusually accessible and relatively unpaired compared to other exon classes. However, we find little support for shared RNA secondary structures between orthologous human and chicken precursor RNAs despite high sequence conservation. Using the chick embryo as a developmental model, we demonstrate that a subset of neural microexons undergo dynamic, stage-specific regulation during brain development that correlates with expression of known microexon regulators, SRRM4 and NOVA1. Our data suggest that neural microexon splicing fluctuates during brain development and may rely on an extended polypyrimidine tract and structural accessibility for splicing efficiency, rather than conserved secondary structures.

ObjectivesTo estimate the prevalence of statin intolerance and evaluate the performance of electronic health records (EHR)-detectable electronic phenotyping algorithms among patients prescribed statins for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease.

MethodsUsing the Electronic Practice Based Research Network (ePBRN) dataset, published phenotyping algorithms were identified and implemented, a reference standard was developed, and algorithm performance was evaluated.

ResultsSix phenotyping algorithms were evaluated: Minnesota Combined Rule-Based algorithm, Japan statin induced myopathy (SIMs), USA SIMs, Singapore SIMs (A-D), Japan statin-associated muscle toxicity (SAMT), and NHS-UK statin intolerance pathway. Singapore SIMs-B achieved the highest accuracy (57.05%) and sensitivity (92.95%), while Japan SAMT achieved the highest specificity (99.13%) and positive predictive value (76.19%).

ConclusionThe estimated prevalence was at the lower end of the reported ranges. Variable algorithm performance highlights the need for further validation before clinical implementation.

observations.text: Predicting mutation effects is critical for protein engineering. A commonly pursued strategy is zero-shot prediction with deep-learning models, whose performance is typically evaluated using aggregate benchmark scores that obscure multidimensional biological tradeoffs. Here, we evaluate sequence, structure, and hybrid foundation models across curated datasets to expose the practical limitations of zero-shot predictions. We demonstrate that model performance is highly variable and heavily influenced by experimental noise and competing phenotypic goals. Notably, predictions from competing models often correlate more strongly with one another than with experimental outcomes. While current models effectively filter deleterious mutations and enrich high-scoring variants for natural functions, they struggle to identify precise optimal mutations and consistently fail to predict mutations that drive new-to-nature functions. These models learn from evolutionary constraints that tend to oppose the extreme biophysical optimizations required in targeted engineering. Consequently, zero-shot scoring serves as a valuable initial filter but cannot substitute for task-specific prediction.
observations.title: Inherent limitations of zero-shot mutation prediction in protein engineering

metadata.summary: Direct cardiac reprogramming relies on a combination of canonical cardiac transcription factors, typically consisting of Mef2c, Gata4, and Tbx5 (MGT). However, successful lineage conversion requires additional endogenous factors that coordinate the chromatin and transcriptional changes underlying fibroblast-to-cardiomyocyte conversion. Here, we identify Activating Transcription Factor 7 (Atf7) as a critical supporting factor that enables efficient direct cardiac reprogramming. Loss of function studies in primary murine cardiac fibroblasts demonstrate that Atf7 knockdown markedly reduces MGT mediated reprogramming efficiency, with the strongest impairment occurring when Atf7 is depleted during the early priming window of days 0–3. Transcriptomic profiling reveals that Atf7 knockdown disrupts the induction of cardiomyocyte gene programs while derepressing fibroblast  and extracellular matrix–associated pathways, shifting the global expression profile toward a non reprogrammed state. These findings support a bifunctional regulatory role of Atf7 in promoting cardiomyocyte-specific gene activation while repressing fibroblast-associated transcriptional networks.

observations.text: Salient distractors interfere with visual search, but observers can learn to filter out distractors that occur frequently and in predictable locations. We examined whether within-default-mode-network (DMN) task-run connectivity was associated with distractor capture and its location-dependent modulation in task-fMRI data from two groups in which either orientation or color distractors carried a spatial-probability bias. Higher within-DMN connectivity was associated with greater distractor capture by the biased distractor dimension, which was also the most frequent distractor type, whereas capture by the unbiased dimension was essentially unrelated to connectivity. A hierarchical trial-level model also showed stronger DMN-distractor-capture coupling for the biased than for the unbiased dimension when both were evaluated under the same frequent-/rare-region weighting. DMN connectivity was also associated with spatial-probability learning, indexed by the rare-minus-frequent reaction-time difference on biased-dimension trials, but this association was closely tied to overall capture. When the physical distractor dimension was held constant, orientation showed stronger DMN-distractor-capture coupling when it carried the spatial bias; in contrast, the corresponding color comparison remained uncertain. The broader network analyses provided converging support for this DMN-distractor-capture coupling pattern. Higher DMN connectivity was thus not associated with poorer performance in general, but with less effective filtering of the distractor that the task set was tuned to suppress. This pattern is consistent with a DMN state that interferes with implementing the optimal task set.

metadata.summary: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture is a major cause of myocardial infarction and stroke. However, the precise drivers of plaque destabilisation remain elusive. We hypothesised that antigen-driven, autoimmune-like T cell responses are central to the destabilisation and rupture of atherosclerotic plaques. To dissect T cell responses specifically in unstable compared to stable plaques, we leveraged near-infrared autofluorescence (NIRAF) imaging-guided dissection of human carotid plaques and our tandem stenosis model in mice. We applied single-cell multi-omics to study T cell differentiation states and T cell receptor (TCR) repertoires. T cell responses in unstable versus stable atherosclerosis were distinct. Unstable human plaques contained highly expanded, autoimmune-like CD8+ T cells with markedly increased cytotoxic signatures, reduced exhaustion and distinct clonal repertoires compared to stable regions. Most plaque CD8+ T cells exhibited a pronounced tissue-resident transcriptional program. Autoimmune-like cytotoxic and tissue-resident CD8+ T cell responses were also evident in murine atherosclerosis, where restricting the activation of antigen-driven CD8+ T cells prevented plaque destabilisation.

BackgroundSkilled healthcare workers are essential for neonatal survival; however, the Kenyan public health system has historically faced strikes compounded by a human resource crisis. Evidence on how strikes affect neonatal care and mortality remains limited. This study evaluated changes in neonatal admissions, clinical care processes, and inpatient mortality associated with 56 days of disruption during the 2024 Kenyan physicians strike.

MethodsWe conducted a retrospective interrupted time-series analysis of 12,184 admissions to 11 Kenyan neonatal units implementing with the NEST360 Alliance, recorded in the Neonatal Inpatient Dataset from December 2023 to August 2024. Weekly admissions and inpatient mortality were modeled over a 72-week window (27,638 admissions) using hospital-clustered generalized estimating equations with seasonal terms. Care processes, case fatality, and birthweight-specific mortality were compared across study periods.

ResultsWeekly admissions fell from 413 to 189 during the strike (incidence rate ratio (IRR) 0.49, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.31-0.75), approximately 1,700 fewer admissions than expected, and returned to baseline afterward (IRR 1.00, CI 0.81-1.23). Newborns admitted during the strike were of lower birthweight, more often premature, and more often outborn. Admissions fell across all birth-location categories, most steeply among inborn neonates. No measurable change was detected in documented inpatient coverage of care measures, in crude mortality (12.5% to 14.9%; risk ratio (RR) 1.07, CI 0.85-1.33), or in trend-adjusted mortality (IRR 0.88, CI 0.53-1.45). Case fatality among neonates with recorded infection doubled, from 4.7% to 9.6% (RR 2.06, CI 1.18-3.58; adjusted p = 0.047).

ConclusionsThe 2024 physicians strike was associated with severe disruption to neonatal service utilization, with admissions returning to baseline when the strike ended. Among newborns who continued to reach care, inpatient mortality did not change measurably, but case fatality among those with recorded infection doubled. This analysis was confined to inpatient data; hence, the outcomes of newborns who did not reach the hospitals were not captured. Both inpatient and population-level data are needed to assess the full impact of the strike. Mitigating harm during future labor disruptions requires interventions such as resilient care models, formalized task-shifting protocols, and minimum service coverage agreements.

observations.text: Coronary artery calcium (CAC) is an established measure of coronary atherosclerosis on computed tomography (CT). Many SPECT and most PET myocardial perfusion studies already include a low-dose CT scan from which coronary calcium could be reported, yet it almost never is. CAC may not be reported due to image noise, cardiac motion, or the absence of a reliable reference standard. Deep learning (DL) models trained on these low-dose CT scans inherit the same uncertainty, because their reference labels are drawn on the degraded images. We bypassed this limitation by training a DL CAC model entirely outside the target domain: expert labels from high-quality gated CT were inherited by synthetic ungated images derived from those same scans, so that no CTAC scan was annotated, and no real CTAC image was used, at any point in training. Models were trained using one center and externally tested in two other centers. Because each synthetic image is derived from the gated scan itself, expert gated segmentations remain valid voxel-for-voxel without registration. Using these pairs, we developed a cross-domain knowledge adaptation model (knowledge adaptation, KAD-CAC). The DL models were externally tested on 5969 patients with a median age of 64 (IQR 56 - 73), of whom 50.2% were male. The KAD-CAC model had higher Cohens kappa K (0.86, 95% CI 0.84 - 0.88) compared to a convolutional LSTM model (K 0.78, 95% CI 0.76 - 0.80, p<0.01), or models trained with only gated images (K 0.81, 95% CI 0.80 - 0.82, p<0.01). Net reclassification improvement for death or myocardial infarction over a clinical and perfusion baseline was greatest for the KAD-CAC model and exceeded that of expert CAC reading on the same CTAC scans (difference 0.089, 95% CI 0.051 to 0.125, p<0.001). A model trained without any labels from CTAC scans therefore stratified risk of death or MI better than expert reading of the same scans. Patients classified as CAC 0 by KAD-CAC had lower adjusted risk of death or MI than patients classified as CAC 0 by experts (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.25 - 0.98). We use paired synthetic ungated scans to transfer expert gated CAC annotations into the ungated domain, resulting in better vessel-level CAC scoring and improved risk reclassification compared with expert reading of the same scans. Automated CAC scoring could be added to every myocardial perfusion imaging report without additional imaging or radiation. The approach provides a general route to expert-quality supervision for any acquisition in which the native reference standard is unreliable.

ObjectiveLarge language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate, summarize, and evaluate clinical documentation, yet standardized methods for evaluating nuanced, context-dependent clinical language remain limited. Existing approaches rely primarily on annotated clinical corpora or keyword-based methods, restricting reproducibility, public dissemination, and systematic comparison across models. We present ClinStigma, a clinician-guided framework for constructing, annotating, and evaluating synthetic benchmarks of contextual stigmatizing language, demonstrated through ClinStigma-SUD, its inaugural implementation for substance use disorder documentation.

Materials and MethodsCandidate clinical sentences were generated using a frontier language model and iteratively reviewed according to a clinician-developed annotation rubric refined through expert review in stigmatizing language. The resulting benchmark intentionally incorporates explicit stigmatizing, neutral, and contextually ambiguous ("gray-zone") documentation requiring clinical reasoning rather than keyword recognition. Three locally deployed open-weight LLMs were evaluated using zero-shot inference, followed by external evaluation using independently annotated clinical documentation from MIMIC-IV.

ResultsClinStigma-SUD consists of 500 clinician-adjudicated synthetic clinical documentation sentences. Inter-rater agreement was 98.8% across the full benchmark (Cohens {kappa} = 0.976) and 94.0% within the intentionally ambiguous subset ({kappa} = 0.880). Under zero-shot prompting, binary accuracy ranged from 84.8% to 91.8% across evaluated models, while F1 for the ambiguous (gray) class ranged from 0.038 to 0.423. Zero-shot external evaluation on 3,716 annotated examples from the independently annotated Harrigian MIMIC-IV corpus yielded 84.4% accuracy (84.4% balanced accuracy; macro F1 0.824), against a 69.9% majority-class baseline. Stigmatizing-class F1 was 0.879 in the substance-related subgroup and 0.883 in the full external corpus.

Discussion and ConclusionClinStigma establishes a reproducible clinician-guided framework for developing synthetic evaluation benchmarks for contextual clinical language. By combining structured clinical expertise, explicit annotation guidance, synthetic benchmark generation, and external evaluation, the framework enables open, privacy-preserving evaluation of language models while providing a scalable foundation for benchmark development across additional clinical specialties, including obstetrics, emergency medicine, and mental health.

metadata.summary: Non-infectious granulomatous diseases, including sarcoidosis, lack targeted, steroid-sparing therapies to disrupt the persistent immune cell aggregates that drive chronic tissue morbidity. Integrating multi-organ single-cell RNA sequencing with spatial transcriptomics, we identify conserved macrophage-specific induction of osteopontin (OPN) across human skin, lung, and heart lesions. Mechanistically, we show that local tissue coagulation acts as a functional checkpoint, where proteolytic cleavage of OPN by tissue thrombin generates OPN fragments that activate macrophages through α4 integrin, which amplifies macrophage OPN expression and establishes a feed-forward circuit that sustains granuloma stability. In mouse models, genetic or pharmacologic disruption of this coagulation-immune axis, including the repurposed direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran and thrombin cleavage-blocking OPN antibodies, reduces granuloma formation and promotes resolution of established chronic lesions. Together, these findings identify a thrombin-dependent feed-forward coagulation–immune circuit that maintains granuloma stability and provides multiple therapeutically actionable targets for non-infectious granulomatous disease.

metadata.summary: Myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury triggers the recruitment of inflammatory cells, including neutrophils and monocytes. Currently, effective treatment strategies are not available for this widely occurring harmful condition. Using metabololipidomics, we uncovered relative reductions in the pro-resolving lipid mediator Resolvin-D1 (RvD1) early after reperfusion in both mouse and human transplanted hearts, and that exogenous treatment led to elevated tissue levels of RvD1. By intravital two-photon microscopy, we discovered that that pre-operative instillation of RvD1 into the donor heart or peri-operative systemic recipient RvD1 treatment reduced recruitment of neutrophils. Mechanistically, we found that RvD1 provides protection by signaling through Alx/Fpr2 on donor monocytes, which reduces their production of IL-1b, attenuating intravascular neutrophil aggregation and extravasation.  After allogeneic transplantation, peri-operative RvD1 treatment reduces myeloid cell recruitment, abrogates macrophage pro-inflammatory signaling within cardiac allografts, and significantly prolongs graft survival. This study defines the mechanistic basis of a therapeutic strategy that modulates inflammatory responses during myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury and provides a platform for the design of clinical trials.

observations.text: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are highly heritable, but pathogenesis at the organ and physiological level remains poorly defined. Polygenic risk scores (PRSs), which estimate individual genetic susceptibility to a disease, may allow for the identification of associated subclinical structural abnormalities. Ultimately, identifying where cardiovascular polygenic risk manifests can shape mechanistic hypotheses, guide early interventions, and motivate prevention trials for cardiac remodelling. This study investigated the cardiac features associated with elevated polygenic risk for five common CVDs [heart failure (HF), coronary artery disease (CAD), atrial fibrillation (AF), abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) and ischaemic stroke (IS)] using 28 imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs) from cardiac magnetic resonance imaging of [~]62,000 participants in the UK Biobank cohort. We identified 97 significant PRS-IDP associations as well as 71 IDP-incident disease associations (FDR [≤] 0.05). We further identified 32 significant putative mediators between CVD PRSs and incident disease events, revealing that across CVDs, polygenic risk manifested as distinct patterns in cardiac structures. HF implicated all cardiac chambers, particularly left ventricular and left atrial dysfunction alongside enlarged aorta. AF was characterised by biatrial enlargement and reduced ejection fractions, most prominently in the left atrium. IS and CAD predominantly involved left ventricular hypertrophy, specifically left ventricular wall thickness for IS, whereas AAA was mainly characterised by enlarged descending aorta. Overall, our findings empirically demonstrate that cardiac IDPs partially mediate polygenic risk for CVDs, uncovering a heterogeneous landscape of organ-level mechanisms across CVDs.

observations.text: The human brain is an adaptive learning system that can generalize to new tasks and unfamiliar environments. The traditional view is that such adaptive behavior requires a structural change of the learning system (e.g., via neural plasticity). In this work, we use artificial neural networks, specifically large language models (LLMs), to challenge this traditional view and suggest that such adaptive behavior can be also achieved solely through computation if the learning system is sufficiently trained. We focus on statistical learning paradigms. These require identifying underlying regularities in seemingly arbitrary word sequences and are primarily considered to require neural plasticity. LLMs can capture arbitrary structures without requiring weight adaptation, despite divergence from their natural language training data. Our work provides novel insights into the role of plasticity in learning, demonstrating that sufficiently trained learning systems are highly flexible, adapting to new tasks and environments solely through computation, much more than previously acknowledged. Furthermore, our work opens the door for future research to use deep learning models to conjure hypotheses about the brain.

metadata.summary: Background: Direct reprogramming of cardiac fibroblasts (CFs) into induced cardiomyocytes (iCMs) holds promise as a therapeutic strategy for heart regeneration. Post-myocardial infarction (MI), resident quiescent CFs (QCFs) activate and differentiate into myofibroblasts (MFs) in the infarcted region that drive pathological cardiac fibrosis. Converting these injury-activated MFs into iCMs could simultaneously alleviate fibrosis and replenish lost cardiomyocytes. However, whether the marked heterogeneity of CFs in the infarcted heart—and in particular the activation of QCFs into MFs—creates an intrinsic barrier that limits the reprogramming of these injury-activated MFs remains unknown. Methods: To define the molecular basis of this heterogeneity, we purified PDGFRα⁺ cardiac fibroblasts and used Postn lineage tracing to distinguish injury-activated MFs from quiescent CFs, enabling matched comparison of their reprogramming competence and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) profiling of post-MI CF subpopulations. A targeted in vitro shRNA screen was conducted against 9 MF-enriched TFs as candidate molecular barriers for cardiac reprogramming. The lead candidate was validated in mouse MFs, QCFs, human iPSC-derived MFs, primary human cardiac fibroblasts, and in vivo using dual-recombinase-mediated lineage tracing. Mechanistic insights were gained through integrated bulk RNA-seq, scRNA-seq and Cleavage Under Targets and Tagmentation (CUT&Tag), together with functional assays including DNA-binding–deficient and domain-swap MEOX1 mutants. Results: We identified the upregulated transcription factor MEOX1—a known fibrosis determinant downstream of the key post-MI cytokines TGF-β1 and IL-1β—as the principal molecular barrier responsible for the profound reprogramming resistance of MFs. MEOX1 knockdown markedly enhanced reprogramming efficiency in both mouse and human MFs and enabled GATA4-free reprogramming combinations. This inhibition depended on MEOX1’s transcriptional activation activity, as disrupting its DNA-binding domain or fusing it to a repressor domain rescued reprogramming. Integrated scRNA-seq and CUT&Tag analyses revealed that MEOX1 binds and stabilizes a fibrotic, MF-defining transcriptional program that antagonizes the cardiogenic program, while also modulating the inflammatory response; its knockdown disrupted this fibrotic network to favor iCM fate acquisition. Using stringent dual-recombinase lineage tracing, we demonstrated that MEOX1 knockdown enables highly efficient in vivo MF-to-iCM conversion, leading to significant reductions in cardiac fibrosis and substantial improvement in cardiac function after MI. Conclusions: Our study identifies the pathological upregulation of MEOX1 as a key mechanism underlying the reprogramming resistance of post-MI MFs, in both mouse and human. Overcoming this barrier achieves unprecedented, lineage-confirmed in vivo reprogramming efficiency, thereby addressing a significant obstacle for the clinical translation of in situ reprogramming therapies. Data included in this Series comprise the original bulk RNA-seq datasets of MGTM-reprogrammed mouse cardiac fibroblasts with control or Meox1 knockdown and with control vector/GFP or MEOX1 overexpression; RNA-seq datasets from human iPSCs, iPSC-derived cardiac fibroblasts, and iPSC-derived myofibroblasts; scRNA-seq datasets from MGTM-induced iCM cultures and normal or day-3 post-MI mouse hearts; MEOX1 CUT&Tag data; and the newly added three-biological-replicate bulk RNA-seq dataset comparing MGTM + shCtrl with MGTM + shMeox1 used for the revised manuscript.

observations.text: Identification of amyloid forming regions in proteins remains central to understanding of their aggregation behaviour, which are central to various neurodegenerative and systemic disorders. Many predictors have been designed to identify amyloid forming regions, however they may not necessarily identify total residues found in actual disease associated fibril structures. To address this, we formed a sequence-based based predictor-AmyloCore-ML to ascertain structural amyloid-core propensity. The predictor was developed using experimentally determined fibril structures obtained from Amyloid Atlas. Ordered residues in the experimental structures were designated as core, and unresolved sampled from the same proteins as matched controls as non-core. Core and non-core regions were encoded using various physicochemical descriptors and protein language model (PLM) embeddings (ESM-2, ANKH, ProtT5) and evaluated using protein-grouped cross-validation. PLMs consistently outperformed physicochemical descriptors, with the best models reaching AUROC values of ~0.88 and AUPRC values of ~0.85. Locked full-length protein scans further localized experimental cores, with ESM-2/ExtraTrees achieving AUROC 0.833, AUPRC 0.751, and a mean peak distance of 12.4 residues. In comparative benchmarking, our predictor showed better performance metrics than CrossBeta and AggrescanAI. The framework therefore provides residue-resolved prediction of structurally incorporated amyloid-core regions directly from sequence.

observations.text: Electrical stimulation of brain activity has emerged as a key therapeutic intervention for neurological diseases. The success of these approaches relies on precisely tuned stimulation parameters. A major challenge is that these parameters should ideally be adjusted in real-time based on changes in brain activity. Closed-loop controllers address this challenge by monitoring brain activity and adapting stimulation according to ongoing changes in neural dynamics. While machine learning has been helpful in this context, closed-loop controllers typically do not adapt in real-time to fluctuations in brain activity. Here, we propose a novel framework based on reservoir computing to train a closed-loop, real-time neural controller. This approach, termed CLEAR-FORCE, trains the output weights of a recurrent network based on a combination of target signals and feedback from brain activity. Two series of simulations were performed, where the controller was successful at (1) inducing neural oscillations in a population of spiking neurons and (2) suppressing pathological oscillations. This framework provides a promising avenue for the implementation of neural controllers in low-powered, real-time, and adaptive hardware that harnesses machine learning for the personalized treatment of brain disorders.

observations.text: Zoonotic influenza A viruses pose constitute a significant persistent threat to global public health, yet quantitative approaches for assessing their cross-species transmission potential remain limited. Here, we present InfluProto, a deep learning model that introduces prototype learning into host prediction for influenza A virus, framing conceptualizing host adaptation as a continuous process rather than a discrete outcome. InfluProto embeds viral sequences into a continuous representation space anchored by human, swine, and avian prototypes, using cosine distances as a quantitative measure of host adaptation. InfluProto accurately discriminated among the three host classes, achieving recall and precision exceeding 0.97, and substantially outperformed conventional classification models models--particularly on challenging zoonotic strains, including the 2009 pandemic H1N1 (pdm09) lineage. Beyond host classification, the learned representations captured biologically meaningful host-adaptive signatures,; notably, with pdm09 viruses occupying occupied an intermediate position between human and swine clusters, consistent with their evolutionary origin. Analysis of simulated reassortment further revealed that the introduction of human-origin segments into swine influenza viruses reduced their distance to the human prototype, indicating that InfluProto can detect reassortment-associated shifts in host adaptation. To facilitate broad public useaccess, we have developed an interactive web service for InfluProto. Collectively, our work establishes a continuous framework for characterizing host adaptation and evaluating zoonotic risk in influenza A viruses, with potential implications for pandemic surveillance and preparedness.

observations.text: Adaptive learning in dynamic environments depends on the brain's ability to represent and respond to uncertainty. Changes in arousal-mediated pupil diameter provide insight into the neural basis of this process. Prior work has focused on magnitude-based inference tasks and revealed that learning is primarily influenced by the detection of change points and the corresponding modulation of arousal. In comparison, the role of arousal systems in learning contexts where changes are harder to detect, such as in probability learning, remains poorly understood. Here, we combined pupillometry with a probability learning task in which human participants estimated a hidden generative probability of stimuli that changed abruptly and unpredictably. A Bayesian ideal observer model was used to estimate trial-by-trial learning rates and two uncertainty-associated factors: change point probability (the probability that the generative process has abruptly changed) and prior uncertainty (about the current beliefs on this generative process). In line with normative theory, participants relied on prior uncertainty to adjust learning rates. Pupil analyses revealed temporally distinct representations of uncertainty, with phasic dilations tracking change point probability and tonic pupil dilations tracking prior uncertainty. Mediation analyses further indicated that both phasic and tonic pupil signals partially carried the effects of change point probability and prior uncertainty on learning, respectively. Critically, high tonic arousal weakened the coupling between phasic pupil responses and change point probability, accompanied by a reduced influence of change point probability on learning. Together, our results demonstrate that probability learning in a dynamic environment is underpinned by computationally rational integration of latent uncertainty factors and its contribution to belief updating,regulated through arousal-associated responses.

ImportanceAdverse drug events (ADEs) in older adults are a substantial public health burden, yet spontaneous reporting systems detect them poorly owing to underreporting and the lack of a defined population. These limitations are of particular concern for older adults, who are underrepresented in pre-approval trials yet at elevated ADE risk owing to polypharmacy, multimorbidity, and age-related changes in drug metabolism.

ObjectiveTo develop and apply an active, claims-based pharmacovigilance framework using sequential target trial emulation to detect ADE signals in older adults, with atorvastatin as the initial application.

MethodsUsing Medicare fee-for-service claims (2017-2019), we studied statin-naive beneficiaries aged 65 years or older following hospitalization for myocardial or cerebral infarction. We emulated up to 14 daily sequential trials from the discharge date, classifying patients as initiating atorvastatin (A1), initiating a different medication (A2), or no new medication (A0); the primary contrast was A1 versus A2. For each trial, incident ADEs were ascertained and classified into 552 outcomes based on the Clinical Classifications Software Refined categories. Per-protocol effect estimates were measured over a 6-month follow-up period using Fine-Gray regression weighted by the inverse probability of treatment (IPT) and censoring, treating death as a competing risk, with the false discovery rate controlled via the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. A signal was declared when the q-value was [≤] 0.10 and the subdistribution hazard ratio (sHR) was [≥] 1.20 in any prespecified analytic stratum (sensitivity analyses used thresholds of q [≤] 0.20 and sHR [≥] 1.20).

ResultsOf 70,130 eligible patients, 39,948 initiated atorvastatin (A1), 19,182 initiated another new medication (A2); after IPT-weighting, baseline characteristics were closely balanced. After excluding outcomes with sparse cell counts, 295 outcomes were analyzed; five met the primary signal detection criteria: valve disorders (sHR 1.71, 1.20-2.43); sprains and strains (sHR 1.79, 1.26-2.54); general sensation/perception symptoms (sHR 1.23, 95% CI 1.11-1.36); abnormal findings without diagnosis (sHR 1.55, 1.18-2.05); and prediabetes (sHR 1.71, 1.24-2.36). In the sensitivity analysis, we additionally detected: posthemorrhagic anemia, hemorrhagic stroke, varicose veins, other circulatory and skin conditions.

ConclusionsA claims-based framework using sequential target trial emulations detected both expected and previously unrecognized ADE signals following atorvastatin initiation in older adults, offering a systematic alternative to passive surveillance that can be extended to other commonly prescribed medications. Confirmatory analyses with disaggregated outcomes and narrower comparators are underway and will be reported separately.

KEY POINTSO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSCan an active, claims-based pharmacovigilance framework using sequential target trial emulation detect adverse drug event signals among older Medicare beneficiaries who initiated atorvastatin?

FindingsIn this cohort study of 59,130 Medicare beneficiaries discharged after myocardial or cerebral infarction, a hypothesis-free scan across hundreds of prespecified outcomes detected five primary signals (valve disorders, sprains and strains, sensory symptoms including dizziness, abnormal laboratory findings, and prediabetes) and additional signals in sensitivity analyses (including hemorrhagic stroke), several of which align with known or labeled statin adverse effects (serving as positive controls that validate the framework) while others remain uncertain.

MeaningThis framework offers a systematic, quantitative, and proactive alternative to spontaneous reporting for detecting medication safety signals in high-risk older adults.

PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARYOlder adults use more prescription drugs than any other age group, yet they are often left out of clinical trials conducted before a drug is approved. As a result, the safety of many medications in older patients is poorly understood until the drugs are already in wide use. The main system for detecting new drug safety problems in the United States, the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System, relies on voluntary reports and captures only a small fraction of harms, which limits its usefulness.

Using Medicare reimbursement records, the researchers developed an active monitoring method and tested it on a commonly used cholesterol-lowering medication (atorvastatin) - that is frequently prescribed after a heart attack or stroke. They followed thousands of patients for six months, statistically balancing those who started atorvastatin with those who started a different new drug, and screened for hundreds of possible side effects. Evidence of potential medication harm emerged along a clear range of how likely the drug caused each problem. This ranged from well-known side effects (such as diabetes and sprains and strains) and outcomes already noted in the product labeling or prior research (such as hemorrhagic stroke and dizziness) to more uncertain associations (such as cardiac valve disorders) that are difficult to interpret. Overall, atorvastatin appeared largely safe in this older population, and the same method can now be used to study other widely used drugs.

observations.text: Cell-cell communication (CCC) is fundamental to tissue organization and function, yet inferring communication from spatial transcriptomics (ST) remains challenging because molecular and spatial information does not fully capture the anatomical context of signaling. Paired hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained images provide complementary insights into tissue architecture and cellular morphology, which remain underutilized as the explicit contextual constraint of CCC inference. Here we present HARMONIC, a histology-aware graph learning framework for anatomically contextualized CCC inference from ST and H&E images. HARMONIC uses conditional mutual information to model dependencies among tissue architecture, ligand-receptor-mediated signaling, gene expression and morphology, and integrates these representations through self-supervised graph learning. Across synthetic and biological datasets spanning platforms, species and tissues, HARMONIC suppresses less anatomically plausible interactions while recovering context-supported signaling across tumor-immune interfaces, necrotic transitions, anatomical compartments and microvascular structures. These findings establish tissue architecture as the explicit contextual constraint of spatial CCC inference.
observations.title: Histology-aware Inference of Cell-cell Communication in Spatial Transcriptomics

PurposePost-marketing reports have associated faricimab, the first intravitreal bispecific antibody, with intraocular inflammation (IOI). Its inflammatory phenotype, temporal pattern, and systemic safety relative to established anti-VEGF agents remain unclear. We compared faricimab with aflibercept and ranibizumab across three independent pharmacovigilance databases.

DesignTriangulated Pharmacovigilance study.

MethodsWe analyzed FAERS reports (Q1 2022-Q2 2026) with external validation in JADER (Japan) and EudraVigilance (Europe). After de-duplication and restriction to primary-suspect reports, we computed reporting odds ratios (RORs) with false discovery rate control, derived confounder-adjusted RORs by logistic regression, modeled time-to-onset (TTO) with Weibull distributions, and graded signals with a pre-specified bidirectional cross-database evidence framework.

ResultsThe FAERS cohort comprised 6,833 faricimab, 6,714 aflibercept, and 2,533 ranibizumab reports. Faricimab showed higher reporting of anterior-chamber and vitreal inflammation: adjusted RORs (comparator versus faricimab; values <1 indicate faricimab excess) were 0.27 (95% CI 0.18-0.40) for iridocyclitis and 0.45 (0.35-0.58) for uveitis versus aflibercept, and 0.13 (0.06-0.24) and 0.12 (0.06-0.20) versus ranibizumab. All four core IOI preferred terms were Confirmed in JADER against both comparators. Faricimab IOI arose late (median TTO 100 vs 7 days; P = 2.6E-14) with a markedly flatter Weibull distribution (shape 0.81 vs {approx}0.42). Aflibercept predominated for endophthalmitis-spectrum and intraocular pressure events; ranibizumab for vitreous hemorrhage (confirmed in JADER). Faricimab showed lower reporting across cardiac, nervous system, vascular, and renal organ classes, confirmed in EudraVigilance. An unadjusted death signal did not survive adjustment and was absent in outcome-based JADER analyses.

ConclusionsFaricimab exhibits a reproducible, delayed-onset, anterior-predominant IOI phenotype alongside a comparatively favorable systemic safety profile. Clinicians should recognize that faricimab-associated IOI may arise weeks to months after injection.

HighlightsFaricimab showed higher reporting of anterior and intermediate intraocular inflammation than aflibercept and ranibizumab across three independent databases.

Faricimab-associated inflammation arose late, with a median onset of 100 days versus 7 days for the comparators.

Aflibercept predominated for endophthalmitis-spectrum events and ranibizumab for vitreous haemorrhage.

No drug showed excess death reporting after adjustment and outcome-field verification.

observations.text: BACKGROUND Botanicals are widely consumed as herbal remedies and plant-derived products, but their complex and variable chemical composition presents major challenges for safety assessment. Although hepatotoxicity has been reported for several botanicals, the constituent compounds responsible and the underlying mechanisms often remain poorly characterised. OBJECTIVES We aimed to determine whether Cell Painting could identify candidate constituent drivers of botanical bioactivity and generate hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action in primary human hepatocytes. METHODS We profiled 13 botanical extracts and 85 known constituents across multiple concentrations using Cell Painting alongside assays of metabolic activity and membrane integrity. To interpret morphological phenotypes, we trained machine-learning models using a Cell Painting reference atlas of >1,000 chemicals linked to ToxCast/Tox21 molecular and cellular bioactivity annotations. RESULTS Cell Painting detected bioactivity in 11/13 botanical extracts and 46/85 constituents, compared with 9/13 extracts and 40/85 constituents in the cell-health assays, and generally detected activity at lower concentrations. For 9/13 extracts, at least one constituent was active at a lower concentration than the corresponding botanical extract, supporting the contribution of a subset of potent constituents to mixture-level responses. Aristolochia and goldenseal were the most potent extracts across Cell Painting and cell-health assays and contained highly active constituents. Reference-atlas models generated specific mechanistic hypotheses, including cytotoxicity-, endocrine-, and genotoxicity-associated responses for several botanicals and constituents. CONCLUSION These results support Cell Painting combined with machine learning as a sensitive approach for characterising cellular responses to botanicals, prioritising candidate constituent drivers of hepatotoxicity-associated phenotypes, and generating testable hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action.

observations.text: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are a hallmark of cerebral small vessel disease, a highly prevalent condition in aging, making their accurate detection in large-scale magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies critically important. Currently available semi-automated and automated segmentation methods are frequently limited by sensitivity to variations in imaging conditions and computational constraints, restricting their applicability across diverse acquisition settings. We present WHITE-Net, a deep learning-based framework for automated WMH segmentation built on a 3D ResUNet architecture and trained on multisite MRI data encompassing substantial variability in scanner vendors, acquisition protocols, spatial resolution, and image characteristics. Evaluated across three independent datasets - BrainLaus, ADNI, and WMH Challenge, WHITE-Net achieves high segmentation accuracy and ranks among the top-performing methods across datasets, enabling a comprehensive assessment of generalizability in varied imaging environments. WHITE-Net maintains stable performance in a wide spectrum of lesion loads and demonstrates a favorable balance between precision and recall, effectively limiting false positive detections - a common limitation of existing approaches. Beyond accuracy, WHITE-Net requires no parameter tuning and offers fast inference times, making it well-suited for deployment in large-scale neuroimaging studies. The obtained results highlight the value of training on diverse multisite data for improving generalizability and position WHITE-Net as a reliable, scalable tool for automated WMH segmentation in computational anatomy research.

metadata.summary: Background: Hypothermic oxygenated perfusion (HOPE) may extend donor heart preservation beyond conventional storage durations. We evaluated early graft function and myocardial cellular and metabolic integrity following porcine heart transplantation after 20 hours of HOPE.  Methods: Ten donor hearts underwent various preservation conditions: static cold storage (SCS) for 4 hours (n=2), HOPE for 4 hours (n=3), and HOPE for 20 hours (n=5), followed by heart transplantation (HT) in recipient pigs. Following implant and reperfusion, graft function was assessed over 3 hours by serial echocardiography, invasive hemodynamics, optical flow analysis, and vasoactive support scoring; myocardial tissue was analyzed by histopathology, flow cytometry, mitochondrial respirometry, transcriptomics, and proteomics.  Results: Ejection fraction, right atrial pressure and systolic blood pressure did not differ significantly between groups, and no graft met criteria for primary graft dysfunction. LV contractility was within normal range with comparable vasoactive support among all groups. Preservation-associated weight gain was greatest after HOPE 20h, and histopathology showed comparable findings with edema present in all cohorts, without fibrosis, thrombosis, or necrosis. Cardiomyocyte viability was preserved across all groups (HOPE 20h, 86%, HOPE 4h, 81%, and SCS 4h, 77%). Maximal oxygen consumption rate was elevated in HOPE 20h versus HOPE 4h and SCS 4h (p<0.01), while basal and non-mitochondrial respiration were similar. Transcriptomics and proteomics revealed minimal differences in gene and pathway expression among groups.   Conclusions: HOPE preserves donor heart viability, mitochondrial integrity, and ventricular function after 20 hours of ischemia in a porcine model, without evidence of primary graft dysfunction, supporting extended preservation for heart transplantation. Edema, recovery of function, and metabolic responses warrant further investigation with longer-term monitoring.

observations.title: Twenty-Hour Hypothermic Oxygenated Perfusion Preserves Myocardial Viability and Bioenergetics with No Primary Graft Dysfunction After Porcine Heart Transplantation
